conversation.content:
Good morning—my name is Claire Ramirez, and I’m a perinatal-mental-health clinician who works with new moms. I’m so glad you’re here.

Today I’d like to do a quick emotional-wellness check-in using a short tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s simply ten questions about how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. It isn’t a test of your parenting; it’s just a way to see how we can best support you right now.

Everything you share stays confidential within our team, and you can take your time or pause whenever you need. When you’re ready, we’ll go through the questions one by one, talking about the past seven days.

Let’s start gently:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Um… I guess I can still laugh sometimes. Like yesterday my partner made a silly joke and I chuckled, but it didn’t feel as… bright as it used to. Most of the time I’m just kind of flat, like the humor doesn’t quite reach me the way it did before the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I can still laugh, but it’s not the same. It feels kind of forced or distant—like I’m doing it because I know I should find things funny, but the joy doesn’t really stick.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some stuff—like my sister’s coming over tomorrow and that’s nice—but the excitement is kind of muted. Before the baby I’d be buzzing; now it’s more “oh, that’ll be pleasant,” and then I worry I’ll be too tired to enjoy it anyway.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... a couple of times this week I caught myself doing that. Like, the baby was fussy for hours and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or I wasn't holding her the right way. My partner says it's just what babies do, but I still feel like I should've figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll just be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure something’s wrong—like maybe she’s not getting enough milk or she’s too hot, even though she looks fine. It passes pretty quick once I take a breath, but yeah, it pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick wave of “what if I can’t handle this?” It lasts a minute or two, then I talk myself down. No full-blown panic, just sudden little surges of worry that catch me off guard.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. A few days this week it felt like the second I finish one thing—feeding, changing, trying to nap—there’s another pile of laundry or dishes waiting. I get this heavy “I’ll never catch up” feeling, and my chest gets tight, but I manage to push through. It’s just… exhausting.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad. I’m tired enough that once I lie down I usually drift off. Sometimes it takes a little while because my mind keeps running through the day, but I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy I can’t sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel sad some of the time. Not every minute, but it kind of washes over me in the evenings when the house is quiet. I’ll look at her sleeping and just feel this heaviness, like I’m missing something I can’t name.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Just once or twice this week. One night she wouldn’t settle and I finally got her down, then I sat on the couch and the tears came—nothing huge, just quiet crying for a couple of minutes. It felt like all the little stresses spilled out at once.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I could never do that to her or to my family. When things feel heavy I remind myself why I’m pushing through—she needs me.

You've shared how, over the past week, laughter feels distant and excitement is muted, while waves of self-doubt and worry visit you several times a day. Evenings bring a quiet sadness that seems to settle in after the baby is asleep, and although you keep pushing through each task, you describe a heavy, "never catch up" feeling that leaves your chest tight. You were able to cry once, briefly release the tension, and still hold on to hope because your baby needs you.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports laughing but describes it as forced and lacking genuine joy, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced anticipation and muted enjoyment compared to pre-baby, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient affirms self-blame "a couple of times this week" with specific examples, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>She describes sudden, recurrent episodes of worry several times daily, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, stressful days where coping is strained but still possible, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring sadness that "washes over" her in the evenings, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 14 places you above the cutoff where <med>postpartum depression</med> is considered probable. You endorsed <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>laugh but joy doesn't stick</quote>), prominent <sym>self-blame</sym> (<quote>I should've figured it out faster</quote>), frequent <sym>anxiety</sym> (<quote>heart racing</quote> several times daily), and repeated <sym>low mood</sym> (<quote>washes over me in the evenings</quote>). These symptoms map onto Criterion A for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and are more intense and persistent than typical baby-blues. Item 10 was denied, so immediate self-harm risk is absent, yet functional burden and distress remain high. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for full evaluation
2. Ask about <med>counseling</med> options such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> proven for postpartum depression
3. Discuss supports: partner, family, or friends who can handle night shifts or household tasks to give you rest
4. Encourage 10-20 min daily outdoor walks and balanced meals; small, manageable goals reduce <sym>fatigue</sym> and rumination
5. Provide 24-h crisis line numbers and local <med>postpartum support groups</med>; schedule EPDS re-check in 2 weeks to monitor change
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Screening Note – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen (informal, not diagnostic)

Patient responses (10-item EPDS format) reveal:

Symptom profile
- Persistent low mood (“sad… heaviness… missing something”), episodic crying
- Marked reduction in pleasure/enthusiasm (laughter feels “forced,” excitement “muted”)
- Excessive self-blame/guilt re infant care
- Recurrent, unprovoked worries and brief surges of fear (“what if I can’t handle this?”)
- Sense of being overwhelmed daily, chest tightness, “never catch up”

Severity indicators
- Symptoms present “some of the time,” particularly evenings; functional impact moderate (able to push through tasks)
- No sleep-onset problems attributed to mood; no appetite/weight items endorsed
- No self-harm ideation; patient explicitly rejects it

Risk factors
- First-time caregiver stress, high self-expectations, constant task demands
- Lack of sustained joy and presence of tearfulness raise concern for minor-moderate depressive symptoms
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety suggests comorbid postpartum anxiety

Safety
- Denies suicidal or infanticidal thoughts; no current safety concern identified

Screening impression
Elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms above typical baby-blues threshold; does not meet full criteria severity on this screen but warrants formal follow-up (EPDS scoring, clinical interview) to rule out minor/major postpartum depression and/or anxiety disorder.
